To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Western Desert of Egypt was substantially wetter than modern conditions during pluvial phases of the Pleistocene, and that tufa deposits from the Kharga Oasis record the effects of evaporation and C4 vegetation in their carbon-isotope compositions, and the effects of evapotranspiration in their oxygen-isotope compositions.

(1) stable isotope analysis of tufas and gastropods from the Kharga Depression, Western Desert of Egypt, indicates that the region received sufficient precipitation to support a perennial lake and substantial spring discharge during the height of stage 6/6e and earlier pluvial phases, (2) the majority of pluvial precipitation was derived from an Atlantic moisture source, (3) the δ13C of tufas suggests a significant contribution of C4 vegetation to spring recharge

the Western Desert of Egypt received enough precipitation to form a small perennial lake and to support substantial spring discharge during the height of stage 6/ 5e, and that spring-carbonate formation in this region required a substantial increase in precipitation relative to modern conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of fossil spring carbonates and gastropods from the hyperarid Western desert of Egypt for paleoclimatic reconstruction.
the use of stable isotopes to reconstruct paleoenvironments in the hyperarid Egyptian Western Desert during the Pleistocene.
the development of a new method of dating tufa deposits, which is based upon the analysis of the oxygen and carbon isotope composition of the tufas themselves.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the oxygen-isotope record of tufas and gastropods from Kharga Oasis provides the first direct evidence of a pluvial climate in central Egypt during oxygen-isotope stages 6, 5e, and perhaps 4.

the tufa deposits in the Western Desert of Egypt are the result of a pluvial climate, which was more humid than today, and which was caused by an increased amount of precipitation from the Atlantic Ocean.

the oxygen-isotope data indicate a substantial increase in precipitation relative to the present, while the carbon-isotope data suggest that the increase in precipitation was not sufficient to eliminate the effects of evaporation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Western Desert of Egypt received enough precipitation to sustain perennial lakes during at least the oxygen-isotope stages 6 and 5e pluvials, but not during the Holocene.
tufa deposits are a useful indicator of past pluvial conditions, but are not a useful indicator of the magnitude of precipitation during pluvial phases.

tufa formation in the Kharga Oasis region was controlled by a combination of high precipitation and low temperatures, which resulted in a high proportion of C4 plants, high spring discharge and low evaporation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Western Desert of Egypt has received enough precipitation to sustain a small, perennial lake and a large spring during the height of pluvial events in the last glacial period.

the Western Desert of Egypt is a region where paleohydrologic conditions can be inferred from spring carbonates, and that this information can be used to constrain the timing of past precipitation events in the region.
stable isotopes of tufa and gastropoda shells can provide a record of the paleo-precipitation and spring discharge in arid environments.
